hints: Look closely at Fig. 6.1 - X points to the small ball-and-stick structure tucked inside the folds, not to the large coiled ribbons themselves.
walkthrough:
Seeing Two Parts To Haemoglobin**
Think of haemoglobin as protein ribbons with something extra held inside. The wide ribbons are the globin polypeptides, and nestled in each one is a small non-protein ring structure. X points to one of those small structures.

Naming The Non-Protein Part**
That iron-containing ring is called the haem group. Each haemoglobin molecule has four of them, one in each subunit.
Final answer: haem (group)

hints: Think about what red blood cells pick up in the lungs and what part of haemoglobin must hold it for the journey.
walkthrough:
What The Haem Is For**
The protein part gives the shape, but the actual loading point is the iron ion ($Fe^{2+}$) in the centre of each haem. In the lungs where $pO_2$ is high, oxygen diffuses in.

Binding One Oxygen**
Each iron binds one $O_2$ molecule reversibly to form oxyhaemoglobin. That is how one haemoglobin can carry up to four oxygens in total.
Final answer: iron in haem combines with / binds one oxygen molecule for transport

hints: Recall primary to quaternary as increasing complexity - what is the new feature that only appears at the quaternary level?
walkthrough:
Beyond One Chain**
Primary, secondary and tertiary structure all describe folding within a single polypeptide. Quaternary is different because it is about how separate polypeptides fit together.

Applying To Haemoglobin**
Haemoglobin has four polypeptides - two alpha and two beta - held together. Having more than one polypeptide chain in the functional molecule is what quaternary means.
Final answer: more than one polypeptide chain associated together

hints: In the lungs haemoglobin must become almost fully loaded, so look for the flat top part of the 5.3 kPa $pCO_2$ curve where saturation is about 95-98%.
walkthrough:
Choosing The Right Curve**
Alveolar air has $pCO_2$ of 5.3 kPa, so use the dashed curve. In the alveoli, blood loads oxygen so saturation must be very high, on the plateau near 95-98%.

Reading Across To $pO_2$**
Trace 95-98% saturation across to the dashed curve and then down to the $pO_2$ axis. You land at about 10-14 kPa, typically around 12 kPa.
Final answer: approx. 10-14 kPa (e.g. about 12 kPa)

hints: Respiring tissues use up oxygen and need haemoglobin to unload, so focus on the lower left part of the graph where saturation is still rising steeply.
Look for the $pO_2$ values where a small fall in $pO_2$ causes a large fall in saturation - that is where unloading happens most readily.
walkthrough:
Where Unloading Happens**
Respiring tissues have low $pO_2$ because oxygen has diffused out and been used in respiration. Haemoglobin arriving there must release much of its oxygen.

Using The Steep Region As Evidence**
Between about 1-6 kPa $pO_2$ the curves are steep. For example on the 5.3 kPa $pCO_2$ curve, saturation falls from about 80% at 6 kPa to about 20% at 1.5 kPa. That large drop shows oxygen is dissociating readily, which is exactly what respiring tissues need.
Final answer: approx. 1-6 kPa; on the steep part of the curve a small decrease in $pO_2$ causes a steep decrease in percentage saturation as haemoglobin releases oxygen

hints: Compare the three curves from left to right at any middle $pO_2$ - which $pCO_2$ curve is lowest and which is highest?
Think about the word for affinity - if saturation is lower at the same $pO_2$, what does that tell you about how tightly haemoglobin holds oxygen?
Pick one $pO_2$ value, e.g. 4 kPa, and read off the % saturation for two different $pCO_2$ values to make a paired comparison with units.
walkthrough:
Describing The Shift**
As $pCO_2$ rises from 2.7 kPa to 5.3 kPa to 10.7 kPa, the whole dissociation curve moves to the right. That means at any given $pO_2$, the percentage saturation is lower.

Linking To Affinity**
Lower saturation at the same $pO_2$ means haemoglobin has a lower affinity for oxygen when $pCO_2$ is high. It holds oxygen less tightly and releases it more easily.

Proving With Numbers**
Always quote a paired comparison with units. For example, at $pO_2$ of 4 kPa, saturation is about 75% when $pCO_2$ is 2.7 kPa, but only about 38% when $pCO_2$ is 10.7 kPa. Notice the gap is large in the middle (2-6 kPa) but the curves converge near 100% at high $pO_2$ of 12-14 kPa.

Final answer: curve shifts to the right as $pCO_2$ increases; percentage saturation decreases / affinity for oxygen decreases; e.g. at $pO_2$ of 4 kPa saturation is about 75% at $pCO_2$ 2.7 kPa but about 50% at $pCO_2$ 5.3 kPa and about 38% at $pCO_2$ 10.7 kPa; difference is large in middle of range and small at high $pO_2$ above about 10 kPa

hints: Recall the named effect where carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions lower haemoglobin affinity to promote unloading in tissues.
walkthrough:
Naming The $pCO_2$ Effect**
The rightward shift caused by increasing $pCO_2$ (and the resulting hydrogen ions from carbonic acid) has a special name. It is called the Bohr shift, also accepted as the Bohr effect.
Final answer: Bohr shift / Bohr effect

hints: Think about which tissues produce most $CO_2$ - highly active tissues - and what they urgently need more of.
Link that extra oxygen supply to the process that releases energy in cells and why it must keep going.
walkthrough:
Matching Supply To Demand**
Active tissues respire faster, so they make more $CO_2$. That high $pCO_2$ lowers haemoglobin affinity exactly where oxygen is needed most, so more oxygen is unloaded.

Keeping Respiration Aerobic**
The extra oxygen allows cells to continue aerobic respiration to release energy. Without it tissues would become anaerobic and produce less ATP.
Final answer: more oxygen released / supplied to respiring tissues to meet increased demand; maintains aerobic respiration
